name: String comparison uses .equals/char == vs reference == on String objects
side_a: No deduct: the hyphen test compares values correctly — either a char comparison (`charAt(i+1) == '-'`, `c == '-'`) or `String.equals` (`substring(i+1,i+2).equals("-")`) — so the detection logic actually fires.
side_b: Deduct: the hyphen test compares a String object with the reference operator `==` (e.g. `username.substring(i+1,i+2) == "-"`), which is never true for a runtime-created substring, so the hyphen is never detected and the required behavior is never performed.

name: Loop consumes/erases characters beyond the delimiter (returned string is missing kept characters) vs. only the delimiter handling differs cosmetically
side_a: no_deduct when every character that must survive into the shortened name is actually appended and returned — i.e., the match branch only disposes of the delimiter itself, and nothing already appended is removed. Cosmetic/syntactic slips in how the character is extracted or compared do not matter.
side_b: deduct when the match branch swallows an extra character besides the delimiter — e.g., an extra `i++` that skips the matched/neighbouring character, or an explicit removal of a character already appended — so the string that is built and returned omits characters the specification requires it to keep. This is an algorithmic defect in *which* pieces are combined, not an excused String-method slip.

name: Loop control that guarantees a runtime failure (never terminates, or indexes past the last character) vs. a loop that always terminates with in-range accesses
side_a: no_deduct when the loop index is advanced on every path and the look-ahead access is guarded (e.g., `i < length - 1`), so the method reliably reaches its return statement with a legal index range; harmless stylistic index arithmetic is ignored.
side_b: deduct when the loop control itself is broken so the method can never return the string: the index is not advanced in one branch (infinite loop), or the bound/look-ahead guarantees an access past the last character (`i <= username.length()`, unguarded `charAt(i + 1)`). This is a loop-logic defect in building the string, distinct from mis-calling a String method.
